title: Doc-V*: Coarse-to-Fine Interactive Visual Reasoning for Multi-Page Document VQA
research_question: Can an OCR-free document agent improve long multi-page visual question answering by actively navigating from coarse document overviews to selectively retrieved high-resolution evidence rather than consuming all pages or a fixed retrieval set?
methodology: Doc-V* formulates multi-page document VQA as a sequential decision process in which a Qwen2.5-VL-based agent first observes global page thumbnails and then chooses among semantic page retrieval, direct page fetching, and final-answer actions while maintaining structured working memory. High-resolution page tokens are cached and injected only when requested, and returned pages retain explicit absolute page identifiers. Training uses supervised fine-tuning on closed-loop expert trajectories followed by GRPO, and evaluation covers five in-domain and out-of-domain document benchmarks using ANLS, F1, and accuracy.

key_findings.finding: The GRPO-trained Doc-V* scored 64.5 on DUDE, 86.2 on MPDocVQA, 77.2 on SlideVQA, 42.1 on MMLongBench-Doc, and 56.3 on LongDocURL, exceeding the corresponding Qwen2.5-VL baseline on every benchmark.
The paper reports an out-of-domain improvement of up to 47.9% over its static RAG baseline.

On MMLongBench-Doc, the full SFT agent achieved 39.8 accuracy while examining 6.4 pages on average; removing retrieval reduced accuracy to 34.9 and increased exploration to 14.2 pages, while removing direct fetching reduced accuracy to 35.2.
Page-level analysis shows complementary behavior: semantic retrieval has higher recall and generally lower precision, while direct page fetching supplies more targeted evidence.
Returned high-resolution page observations are explicitly prefixed with absolute page identifiers, preserving an unambiguous page-to-evidence mapping even when pages are fetched out of order.
Ablating the global thumbnail overview, page-by-page analysis, or working memory degraded performance on all three reported ablation benchmarks.

limitations: All experiments use a single vision-language backbone, Qwen2.5-VL, so backbone generality is not experimentally established.
Evaluation is restricted to single-document scenarios rather than evidence aggregation across multiple heterogeneous documents.
The framework may produce incorrect or incomplete answers because of hallucination or imperfect evidence aggregation.
Evidence provenance is principally page-level: retrieval and fetch actions identify pages, but the framework does not provide evaluated grounding to precise within-page regions or spreadsheet cells.
The study does not model temporal document versions or cross-version element lineage.
raw_claims: Doc-V* treats multi-page document question answering as sequential visual evidence acquisition.
The initial observation contains page thumbnails annotated with absolute page numbers.
The agent can search semantically for pages, fetch pages by absolute index, or terminate with an answer.
High-resolution visual tokens are cached and supplied selectively rather than all at once.
Each returned page is associated with an explicit absolute page identifier.
Training begins with supervised imitation of closed-loop expert trajectories and continues with GRPO.
The raw training data comes from MP-DocVQA and DUDE.
Evaluation uses two in-domain and three out-of-domain document benchmarks.
The GRPO model improved over the direct Qwen2.5-VL baseline on all five reported benchmark columns.
Retrieval and direct fetching are empirically complementary rather than interchangeable.
The authors restrict evaluation to single-document reasoning and one backbone.
